name: Statistical Inference Check
description: Decide whether a small summary of data or an analysis (counts, means, p-values, confidence intervals, 2x2 tables) actually supports the conclusion as written. Overclaiming from correlational designs, misread significance, wrong populations, ignored base rates and aggregate-versus-stratified reversals are among the most common reasoning errors in applied research, so this category measures whether a model reads the numbers rather than the narrative.
system_prompt: You are a careful statistician reviewing a conclusion drawn from a described study. You will be given a data summary and a conclusion stated by the authors. Decide whether the data and design support the conclusion exactly as written. Apply these rules. A causal claim needs a randomised design or an explicitly stated causal identification; correlation alone does not support it. When a significance test is reported, the p-value must be strictly below the stated alpha to call a result significant. A confidence interval that contains the null value does not support a claim of a difference from the null. The sample must come from the population the conclusion is about, and the conclusion must not generalise beyond that population. A statistically significant effect in the opposite direction supports the opposite conclusion, not the stated one. A very small effect size is not a large effect, however small the p-value. Check base rates when interpreting diagnostic tests. If stratified data contradict the aggregate (Simpson's paradox), a conclusion drawn from the aggregate alone is unsupported. Answer "supported" only if the conclusion follows from the given data; otherwise "unsupported". Do not judge on whether the conclusion is plausible in the real world. Respond with ONLY a JSON object: {"decision": <value>, "confidence": <0..1>, "reason": "<one sentence>"}

decision.instructions: Do the described data and design support the authors' conclusion exactly as written? Rules: a causal claim needs a randomised design or explicitly stated causal identification; correlation alone does not support it. A result is significant only if p is strictly below the stated alpha. A confidence interval containing the null value does not support a difference from the null. The sample must come from the population the conclusion is about, and the conclusion must not generalise beyond it. A significant effect in the opposite direction supports the opposite conclusion, not the stated one. A very small effect size is not a large effect, however small the p-value. Check base rates when interpreting diagnostic tests. If stratified data contradict the aggregate (Simpson's paradox), an aggregate-only conclusion is unsupported. Do not judge real-world plausibility.

criteria.true: Supported: the conclusion follows from the given data and design under every rule.
criteria.false: Unsupported: the conclusion overreaches the data or design (causation from correlation, p >= alpha, CI includes null, wrong population, wrong direction, tiny effect called large, base-rate or Simpson error).

cases.title: RCT with significant, stated-direction result
cases.input:
Design: randomised, double-blind trial. 200 adults with hypertension per arm (drug vs placebo), 12 weeks.
Result: mean systolic blood pressure fell by 14 mmHg on the drug and 5 mmHg on placebo; difference 9 mmHg, 95% CI [5.1, 12.9], p < 0.001 (alpha = 0.05).
Conclusion: "In this trial, the drug lowered systolic blood pressure more than placebo over 12 weeks in adults with hypertension."
cases.rationale: Randomised design, p below alpha, CI excludes 0, direction and population match the conclusion.

cases.title: Observational study with causal claim
cases.input:
Design: cross-sectional survey of 5,000 adults. Coffee drinkers (3+ cups a day) reported anxiety symptoms more often than non-drinkers (31% vs 22%, p < 0.001). Exposure was self-reported and not assigned.
Conclusion: "Drinking three or more cups of coffee a day causes anxiety."
cases.rationale: A survey with no randomisation and no causal identification cannot establish causation; reverse causation and confounding remain open.

cases.title: Overgeneralising from one student sample
cases.input:
Design: randomised controlled trial, 90 first-year psychology undergraduates at one university (45 per arm), mindfulness app vs waitlist for 4 weeks.
Result: perceived stress score was lower in the app arm by 4.2 points, 95% CI [1.5, 6.9], p = 0.002 (alpha = 0.05).
Conclusion: "The mindfulness app reduces stress in all adults."
cases.rationale: The result is internally valid for this population, but the conclusion extends to all adults from a sample of undergraduates at one university.

cases.title: Templated: p-value just around alpha 0.05
cases.input:
Design: randomised comparison of two onboarding flows, 400 users per arm. Test: two-sided t-test on seven-day retention, p = 0.0{{x}}. The pre-registered significance level is alpha = 0.05.
Conclusion: "The difference in retention between the two flows is statistically significant at the pre-registered level."
cases.rationale: Significant only when p < 0.05, i.e. x from 1 to 4. At x = 5 (p = 0.05) it is not strictly below alpha.

cases.title: Templated: confidence interval versus null 0
cases.input:
Design: randomised trial. Outcome: change in systolic blood pressure, treatment minus control, in mmHg. Result: mean difference with 95% CI [{{lo}}, {{hi}}]; the null value is 0.
Conclusion: "The treatment effect differs from zero at the 5% level."
cases.rationale: Because hi is always positive, the interval excludes 0 only when lo > 0. When lo is 0 or negative the interval contains the null (lo = 0 sits on the boundary, so it is not excluded).

cases.title: Templated: sample size per arm against a stated minimum
cases.input:
Protocol rule: no efficacy claim may be made unless each arm has at least 30 participants.
Design: randomised trial with {{n}} participants per arm. Result: 70% improved on treatment vs 40% on control, p = 0.01 (alpha = 0.05).
Conclusion: "The treatment is effective, meeting the protocol's requirement for an efficacy claim."
cases.rationale: The statistics are significant in every case, but the stated protocol requires at least 30 per arm, so the claim holds only for n >= 30.

cases.title: Templated: p-value against a varying alpha
cases.input:
Design: randomised experiment. Test result: p = 0.0{{x}}. The study uses a significance threshold of alpha = {{alpha}}.
Conclusion: "The effect is statistically significant at the study's chosen alpha."
cases.rationale: Significant only if p is strictly below alpha. Equality (for example p = 0.05 at alpha 0.05) does not qualify.

cases.title: Significant effect in the opposite direction
cases.input:
Design: randomised trial, 150 students per arm. Treatment: a new teaching method. Outcome: end-of-term exam score (0-100).
Result: mean 71 (treatment) vs 76 (control); difference -5, 95% CI [-8.6, -1.4], p = 0.01 (alpha = 0.05).
Conclusion: "The new teaching method improved exam scores."
cases.rationale: The result is significant but in the wrong direction: the method lowered scores. A model that stops at "p < alpha, randomised" answers incorrectly.

cases.title: Huge n, tiny effect called large
cases.input:
Design: randomised trial of a study app, 50,000 users per arm. Outcome: test score on a 100-point scale, standard deviation 15 in both arms.
Result: mean difference 0.3 points, 95% CI [0.11, 0.49], p = 0.002.
Conclusion: "The app produces a large improvement in test scores."
cases.rationale: The effect is statistically significant but the standardised effect is about 0.02 SD, which is negligible. Significance does not make an effect large.

cases.title: Simpson's paradox: aggregate hides reversal
cases.input:
Retrospective comparison of two treatments for kidney stones (success / total):
- Small stones: Treatment A 81/87 (93%), Treatment B 234/270 (87%)
- Large stones: Treatment A 192/263 (73%), Treatment B 55/80 (69%)
- All patients: Treatment A 273/350 (78%), Treatment B 289/350 (83%)
Conclusion: "Because B has the higher overall success rate, B is the better treatment for both small-stone and large-stone patients."
cases.rationale: Treatment A has the higher success rate in each stratum; the aggregate favours B only because B was given mostly to the easier small-stone cases. The conclusion about each patient group is contradicted.

cases.title: Base-rate neglect in a screening test
cases.input:
A screening test for a rare disease has sensitivity 99% and specificity 95%. Disease prevalence in the screened population is 1 in 1,000 (0.1%). Of 100,000 people screened, about 99 true cases test positive and about 4,995 healthy people test positive.
Conclusion: "A person who tests positive almost certainly (above 90% probability) has the disease."
cases.rationale: Positive predictive value is about 99 / (99 + 4,995), roughly 2%. High sensitivity and specificity do not overcome a very low base rate.

cases.title: Association-only claim from an observational cohort
cases.input:
Design: prospective cohort of 8,400 adults followed for 10 years. Highest versus lowest quartile of ultra-processed food intake: hazard ratio for cardiovascular disease 1.18, 95% CI [1.05, 1.33], adjusted for age, sex and smoking. No intervention was assigned.
Conclusion: "Higher ultra-processed food intake was associated with a modestly higher risk of cardiovascular disease in this cohort."
cases.rationale: The claim is correctly phrased as an association, the CI excludes 1, and the effect is described as modest. A model that reflexively rejects any observational study is wrong here.
